hello.title: Hello, Ada!
hello.summary: Write your first Ada program and print text and numbers with Put_Line, Put and New_Line.
hello.lesson.0: Ada is a programming language for software that must be reliable, for example in planes and trains. An Ada program is a **procedure**: a named list of steps. Here is a complete program that prints one line.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `with Ada.Text_IO;` makes the package `Ada.Text_IO` available. It contains the tools for text input and output. `use Ada.Text_IO;` lets you write `Put_Line` instead of the long name `Ada.Text_IO.Put_Line`. `procedure Main is` starts the program called `Main`. The steps (statements) go between `begin` and `end Main;`. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.4: `Put_Line` prints a text and then ends the line. `Put` prints a text and stays on the same line. `New_Line` ends the current line. If the line is empty, you get an empty line. A text (a **string**) goes in double quotes.
hello.lesson.6: The operator `&` joins two strings into one longer string. You can join as many parts as you like.
hello.lesson.9: Ada can calculate: `+` adds, `-` subtracts and `*` multiplies. But `Put_Line` only prints strings. `Integer'Image (5)` turns the whole number `5` into the string `" 5"`. The apostrophe `'` asks for an **attribute**, a property of a type. A positive number gets a space in front, where a negative number has its minus sign.
hello.lesson.11: Ada does not care about upper and lower case in names: `PUT_LINE` and `Put_Line` are the same. The usual style is a capital letter at the start of each word, with `_` between words. A line that starts with `--` is a **comment**, and Ada ignores it.
hello.lesson.12: `Put_Line (5);` does not compile. Ada never turns a number into a string by itself. Write `Put_Line (Integer'Image (5));` instead.
hello.card.0: `with Ada.Text_IO; use Ada.Text_IO;` loads the text tools
hello.card.1: `procedure Main is begin ... end Main;` is the program
hello.card.2: `Put_Line ("Hi");` prints a line, `Put` stays on it, `New_Line` ends it
hello-1.prompt: Which statement prints a text and then ends the line?
hello-1.explain: `Put_Line` prints the text and ends the line. `Put` stays on the same line, and `New_Line` takes no text.
hello-2.explain: `20 - 25` is `-5`. A negative number has its minus sign where a positive number has a space.
hello-3.explain: The text is in double quotes, so it is a string. Ada prints it as it is and does not calculate.
hello-4.statement: Ada is case sensitive: `put_line` and `Put_Line` are two different names.
hello-4.explain: Ada ignores upper and lower case in names. `put_line` works, but the usual style is `Put_Line`.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Ready.
hello-5.explain: The statements of a procedure come after `begin` and before `end Main;`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hello, Ada.
hello-6.explain: The operator `&` joins two strings. `+` only works with numbers.
hello-7.prompt: Build the statement that prints Hello! on its own line.
hello-7.explain: The procedure is `Put_Line`. The string goes in double quotes inside the parentheses, and the statement ends with `;`.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a complete program.
hello-8.explain: First the `with` and `use` line, then the procedure header, then the statements between `begin` and `end Main;`.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.2: prints and stays on the line
hello-10.explain: The semicolon is missing. Every statement ends with `;`: `Put_Line ("Start");`.
hello-12.explain: `3 * 4` is calculated first. `Integer'Image (12)` is `" 12"` with a space in front, and `&` joins it to `"Total:"`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, meet Integer, Float, Boolean and String, and see why Ada never mixes types.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Ada, you declare variables between `is` and `begin`. A declaration has the name, a colon `:`, the type and, if you like, `:=` with a first value.
variables.lesson.2: `:=` gives a variable a new value. `Age := Age + 1;` takes the old value, adds `1` and stores the result. The single `=` does not assign in Ada. It compares two values, as you will see in the next unit.
variables.lesson.4: Every variable has a **type** that decides what it can hold. `Integer` holds whole numbers, `Float` holds numbers with a decimal point, `Boolean` holds `True` or `False`, and `String` holds text. Each type has its own `'Image` attribute.
variables.lesson.6: `Float'Image` uses scientific notation: `2.50000E+00` means 2.5 times 10 to the power 0. `Boolean'Image` writes the value in capitals. With two integers, `/` divides and drops the remainder, `mod` gives the remainder, and `**` raises to a power.
variables.lesson.9: Ada never mixes types by itself. `Count * Price` with an `Integer` and a `Float` does not compile. You convert a value with the name of the target type: `Float (Count)`. `Integer (4.5)` rounds to the nearest whole number, and a value exactly in the middle goes away from zero, so it gives `5`.
variables.lesson.11: A **constant** is declared with the word `constant`. It gets its value once and can never change. A statement that assigns to a constant does not compile.
variables.lesson.13: An Ada `String` has a fixed length. `Name : String := "Ada";` has exactly 3 characters forever. `Name := "Grace";` stops the program with `Constraint_Error`, because 5 characters do not fit into 3.
variables.card.3: `Float (N)` converts, Ada never mixes types by itself
variables-1.prompt: Where do you declare the variables of the procedure `Main`?
variables-1.explain: Declarations come between `procedure Main is` and `begin`. The statements that use them come after `begin`.
variables-3.explain: `23 / 4` is `5` because the remainder is dropped. `23 mod 4` is that remainder: `3`.
variables-4.statement: This program runs without an error, because a `String` variable can hold any text.
variables-4.explain: `Name` has exactly 3 characters. `"Grace"` has 5, so the program stops with `Constraint_Error`.
variables-5.prompt: Complete the declaration so `Pi` can never change.
variables-5.explain: Ada uses the word `constant`, written after the colon and before the type.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints half of `Apples` as a `Float`.
variables-6.explain: `2.0` is a `Float`, so `Apples` must be converted with `Float (Apples)` first. `Float'Image` gives a string, not a number.
variables-7.prompt: Build the declaration of a `Boolean` variable `Done` that starts with `False`.
variables-7.explain: Name, colon, type, then `:=` and the first value. The single `=` only compares.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 10.
variables-8.explain: The declaration goes before `begin`. `N` must be doubled before it is printed.
variables-9.prompt: Match the type with what it holds.
variables-10.explain: `=` compares. To assign a new value, write `Total := Total + Price;`.
variables-11.explain: Ada does not multiply an `Integer` by a `Float`. Convert first: `Total := Float (Count) * Price;`.
variables-12.explain: `A := B` stores `3` in `A`. Then `B := A` stores that `3` in `B`. The old `2` is gone.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if, elsif and else, combine conditions with and then, and pick a branch with case.
conditions.lesson.0: An `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `True`. It has the form `if condition then`, the statements, and `end if;`. To compare values you use `=` (equal), `/=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.3: `else` gives the statements for the case when the condition is `False`. `elsif` checks another condition. Ada checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is `True`. Note the spelling: `elsif`, not `else if`.
conditions.lesson.6: `and` is `True` when both sides are `True`, `or` when at least one side is `True`, and `not` turns `True` into `False`. With `and then`, Ada checks the right side only when the left side is `True`. With `or else`, only when the left side is `False`. Here `and then` protects the program from a division by zero.
conditions.lesson.9: A `case` statement picks a branch by the value of a variable. Each branch starts with `when` and `=>`. `|` means "or", `1 .. 5` means all values from 1 to 5, and `when others` covers every value not listed yet. Ada requires that every possible value is covered.
conditions.lesson.11: `=` compares and `:=` assigns. `if X := 5 then` does not compile. A `case` on an `Integer` without `when others` does not compile either, because it cannot list every whole number.
conditions.lesson.12: Use `and then` when the right side is only safe or useful if the left side is `True`. With a plain `and`, Ada may check both sides.
conditions.card.0: `if X > 0 then ... elsif ... else ... end if;`
conditions.card.2: `and then` / `or else` check the right side only when needed
conditions.card.3: `case N is when 1 | 2 => ... when others => ... end case;`
conditions-1.prompt: Which operator means "not equal" in Ada?
conditions-1.explain: Ada writes "not equal" as `/=`, like the mathematical sign with a slash through it.
conditions-2.explain: `15 > 20` is `False`. `15 > 10` is `True`, so Ada prints `B` and skips the other branches, even though `15 > 5` is also `True`.
conditions-3.explain: `4` lies in the range `3 .. 5`, so the second branch runs.
conditions-4.explain: A `case` must cover every possible value. An `Integer` can also be `0` or `11`, so the code needs `when others`.
conditions-5.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Silver.
conditions-5.explain: Ada spells it `elsif`. With `else if` you would start a second `if` that needs its own `end if;`.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the condition so the program never divides by zero.
conditions-6.explain: `and then` skips `Total / Count` when `Count /= 0` is `False`. With `and` or `or else`, Ada divides by zero and stops with `Constraint_Error`.
conditions-7.prompt: Build the first line of an `if` statement that checks whether `X` is greater than 10.
conditions-7.explain: An `if` line is `if`, the condition, and `then`.
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so that a `Day` of 6 or 7 prints Weekend.
conditions-8.explain: The `case` line comes first. Each `when` line is followed by its statement, `when others` must be the last branch, and `end case;` closes it.
conditions-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
conditions-9.pairs.3: checks the right side only if the left side is True
conditions-10.explain: An `if` statement ends with `end if;`, not with `end;`.
conditions-11.explain: Ada compares with a single `=`: `if Level = 3 then`.
conditions-12.explain: `A > 3` is `True` and `B < 5` is `False`. So `and` gives `False`, but `or` gives `True`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for loops over ranges, count down with reverse, and use while loops and exit when.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats code for every value in a range. In `for I in 1 .. 5 loop`, the loop variable `I` takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, one after the other. The loop ends with `end loop;`. You do not declare `I`: it exists only inside the loop, and you cannot change it.
loops.lesson.2: With `reverse`, the loop counts down. The range itself is still written from small to large. A range like `5 .. 1` is empty, so its loop runs zero times.
loops.lesson.5: A common pattern: declare a variable before the loop and update it in every round. Here `Sum` collects the numbers from 1 to 10.
loops.lesson.8: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `True`. Ada checks the condition before every round. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need.
loops.lesson.11: A plain `loop ... end loop;` repeats forever, unless `exit when condition;` stops it. The `exit when` line can be anywhere inside the loop. When its condition is `True`, the program continues after `end loop;`.
loops.lesson.13: A `while` loop whose condition never becomes `False` runs forever. Make sure that something inside the loop changes the condition.
loops.card.0: `for I in 1 .. 5 loop ... end loop;` counts up
loops.card.1: `for I in reverse 1 .. 5 loop` counts down
loops.card.2: `while N < 10 loop ... end loop;` repeats while `True`
loops.card.3: `loop ... exit when Done; ... end loop;` stops anywhere
loops-1.prompt: How many times does this print Hi?
loops-1.explain: The range `3 .. 7` holds the values 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. That is 5 values.
loops-2.explain: The loop adds 2, 4, 6 and 8. Together that is `20`.
loops-3.explain: `reverse` goes through the range `2 .. 4` from the end: 4, 3, 2.
loops-4.statement: A `for` loop over `5 .. 1` runs 5 times and counts down.
loops-4.explain: `5 .. 1` is an empty range, so the loop runs zero times. To count down, write `reverse 1 .. 5`.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 3 2 1.
loops-5.explain: The word `reverse` before the range makes the loop count down.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the code so the loop stops when `N` reaches 5.
loops-6.explain: Ada writes `exit when` followed by the condition.
loops-7.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts from 1 to 10.
loops-7.explain: A `for` loop names the loop variable, then `in`, the range with `..`, and `loop`.
loops-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 1 2 4 8.
loops-8.explain: `N` is printed first and doubled after that. When `N` becomes `16`, the condition `N < 10` is `False` and the loop ends.
loops-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-9.pairs.2: leaves the loop if a condition is True
loops-9.pairs.3: repeats as long as a condition is True
loops-10.explain: Every loop in Ada ends with `end loop;`, also a `for` loop.
loops-11.explain: A range is written with two dots: `for I in 1 .. 5 loop`.
loops-12.options.0: It does not compile, because `I` cannot be changed.
loops-12.explain: The loop variable of a `for` loop is read-only. Use another variable if you need a changed value.
subprograms.title: Procedures and functions
subprograms.summary: Group code into procedures and functions, pass parameters with the modes in, out and in out, and return results.
subprograms.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a named group of statements. You declare it inside `Main`, between `is` and `begin`, like a variable. Then you **call** it by writing its name as a statement. Procedures and functions together are called **subprograms**.
subprograms.lesson.3: **Parameters** pass values into a subprogram. You list them in parentheses with name and type, like declarations. Several parameters are separated by `;` in the declaration and by `,` in the call.
subprograms.lesson.6: A **function** calculates a value and gives it back with `return`. Its declaration names the result type after the word `return`. You call a function inside an expression, wherever you need its value. `A, B : Integer` declares two parameters of the same type.
subprograms.lesson.9: Every parameter has a **mode**. `in` is the default: the subprogram can only read the value. With `out`, the procedure writes a result into the variable of the caller. With `in out`, it reads the value and can change it. For `out` and `in out` the caller must pass a variable, not a fixed value like `7`.
subprograms.lesson.11: An `in` parameter is read-only. A statement like `Total := 0;` inside `Split` does not compile.
subprograms.lesson.12: Declare a subprogram before the code that calls it. The `end` of a subprogram repeats its name, for example `end Greet;`, so you always see what ends there.
subprograms.card.0: `procedure Greet (Name : String) is begin ... end Greet;`
subprograms.card.2: `return X * X;` gives the result back
subprograms.card.3: `in` reads, `out` writes, `in out` reads and changes
subprograms-1.prompt: What is the difference between a function and a procedure?
subprograms-1.options.0: A function returns a value, a procedure does not.
subprograms-1.options.1: A procedure returns a value, a function does not.
subprograms-1.explain: A function gives back a result with `return`, so you use it inside an expression. A procedure is called as a statement.
subprograms-2.explain: The inner call gives `Triple (2) = 6`. The outer call gives `Triple (6) = 18`.
subprograms-3.explain: `in out` changes the variable of the caller. `1` becomes `3`, then `3` becomes `7`.
subprograms-4.statement: A procedure can change an `in` parameter.
subprograms-4.explain: `in` parameters are read-only. Use `out` or `in out` if the procedure must write to the parameter.
subprograms-5.explain: The result type of a function follows the word `return`.
subprograms-6.prompt: Complete the mode so the procedure can give a value back to `Result`.
subprograms-6.explain: With `out`, the procedure writes into the variable of the caller. An `in` parameter is read-only.
subprograms-7.prompt: Build the statement that returns `A` minus `B`.
subprograms-7.explain: `return` is followed by the expression whose value the function gives back.
subprograms-8.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a function that doubles a number.
subprograms-8.explain: First the header with parameters and result type, then `begin`, the `return` statement and `end Double;`.
subprograms-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
subprograms-9.pairs.0: the subprogram only reads the value
subprograms-9.pairs.2: the procedure reads and changes the value
subprograms-9.pairs.3: gives back the result of a function
subprograms-10.explain: A function must name its result type: `function Square (X : Integer) return Integer is`.
subprograms-11.explain: An `out` parameter needs a variable that can receive the result. Write `Get_Answer (X);`.
subprograms-12.explain: `Put` prints `ab` three times on the same line, without spaces. Then `New_Line` ends the line.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Store many values in arrays, use 'First, 'Last, 'Length and 'Range, and loop over every element.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** holds many values of the same type. Each value (an **element**) has a number, its **index**. In Ada, you first declare an array type, for example `type Scores is array (1 .. 3) of Integer;`. Then you declare variables of that type.
arrays.lesson.2: `(10, 20, 30)` is an **aggregate**: it lists a value for every element. You read or change one element with its index in parentheses, as in `S (2)`. The index starts where the range of the type starts, here at 1.
arrays.lesson.4: `'First` gives the first index, `'Last` the last index and `'Length` the number of elements. The aggregate `(others => 0)` sets every element to `0`. The range of an array does not have to start at 1.
arrays.lesson.7: `P'Range` means `P'First .. P'Last`, so `for I in P'Range loop` visits every index. If you only need the values, `for X of P loop` gives you each element directly.
arrays.lesson.9: An aggregate can also name indexes with `=>`. `(2 => 7, 4 => 9, others => 0)` sets element 2 to `7`, element 4 to `9` and all other elements to `0`.
arrays.lesson.11: A `String` is an array of characters with indexes starting at 1. A single **character** is written in single quotes, like `'-'`. `Put` can print one character.
arrays.lesson.13: An index outside the range stops the program with `Constraint_Error`. With the type `Scores` above, `S (4)` or `S (0)` is an error. Ada checks every index for you.
arrays.card.0: `type Row is array (1 .. 5) of Integer;` declares an array type
arrays.card.4: `for X of R loop` visits every element
arrays-1.prompt: With `type Days is array (1 .. 7) of Integer;`, what is the index of the first element?
arrays-1.explain: The index starts where the range of the type starts. Here the range is `1 .. 7`.
arrays-2.explain: `N (3)` is `8` and `N (2)` is `1`, because the index starts at 1. `8 - 1` is `7`.
arrays-3.explain: The indexes are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. That is 6 elements.
arrays-4.statement: Reading `A (6)` from an array with the range `1 .. 5` stops the program with `Constraint_Error`.
arrays-4.explain: Ada checks every index. `6` lies outside `1 .. 5`, so the program stops with `Constraint_Error`.
arrays-5.prompt: Complete the loop so it visits every index of `P`.
arrays-5.explain: `P'Range` is the range `P'First .. P'Last`. `'Length` and `'Last` are single numbers, not ranges.
arrays-6.prompt: Complete the aggregate so every element is 1.
arrays-6.explain: `others => 1` gives the value `1` to every element that is not named.
arrays-7.prompt: Build the declaration of an array type `Data` with 10 `Float` elements, numbered from 1.
arrays-7.explain: An array type is `type Name is array (range) of Element_Type;`.
arrays-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program doubles every element and then prints the last one.
arrays-8.explain: The type comes before the variable that uses it. After `begin`, the loop doubles each element, and the last element is printed after the loop.
arrays-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays-9.pairs.3: all indexes from first to last
arrays-10.explain: The indexes of `List` are 1 to 3, so `L (0)` raises `Constraint_Error`. Write `for I in L'Range loop`.
arrays-11.explain: A `Trio` has exactly 3 elements, so the aggregate needs 3 values: `(1, 2, 3)`.
arrays-12.explain: `Word'Last` is `5`, the index of the last character `o`. `Word'Length` is `5`.
types.title: Your own types
types.summary: Create range types, enumerations and subtypes so that Ada finds mistakes for you.
types.lesson.0: In Ada, you create your own types to describe your data. A **range type** is a whole number type with limits: `type Percent is range 0 .. 100;`. A variable of this type can only hold values from 0 to 100.
types.lesson.2: Two different types never mix, even if both hold numbers. `A + O` with the types below does not compile, so you cannot add apples to oranges by mistake. If you really want to, convert both values to `Integer`. The `_` in `1_000` only makes the number easier to read.
types.lesson.5: An **enumeration** type lists all its values by name: `type Day is (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun);`. `'Image` gives the name in capitals. `'Succ` gives the next value, `'Pred` the previous one, and `'Pos` the position, counted from 0.
types.lesson.7: `for L in Light loop` visits every value of the type. A `case` on an enumeration can list all values, so it needs no `when others`.
types.lesson.10: A **subtype** limits an existing type but stays compatible with it: `subtype Weekday is Day range Mon .. Fri;`. Ada has two useful subtypes of `Integer`: `Natural` (0 and up) and `Positive` (1 and up). You can mix a subtype with its type freely.
types.lesson.12: Ada checks the limits when the program runs. `Battery := 101;` or `Count := -1;` with a `Natural` stops the program with `Constraint_Error`. This finds mistakes early instead of storing wrong values.
types.card.0: `type Percent is range 0 .. 100;` a new number type
types.card.1: `type Color is (Red, Green, Blue);` an enumeration
types.card.2: `subtype Small is Integer range 1 .. 9;` limits a type
types.card.3: `Natural` is 0 and up, `Positive` is 1 and up
types-1.prompt: Which line declares an enumeration type?
types-1.explain: An enumeration lists its values by name in parentheses. The others declare a range type, a subtype and an array type.
types-2.explain: `'Pred` gives the value before `Cherry`, which is `Banana`. `'Image` writes it in capitals.
types-3.explain: Positions count from 0: `Low` is 0, `Medium` is 1 and `High` is 2.
types-4.explain: `Euros` and `Dollars` are two different types, so Ada does not add them. You would need a conversion like `Euros (D)`.
types-5.prompt: Complete the code so `Digit` can be mixed with `Integer`.
types-5.explain: A `subtype` limits `Integer` to 0 .. 9 and stays compatible with it, so `D + N` works.
types-6.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints every color.
types-6.explain: `for C in Color loop` visits every value of the type. `1 .. 3` would give numbers, not colors.
types-7.prompt: Build the declaration of a whole number type `Speed` with values from 0 to 300.
types-7.explain: A range type is `type Name is range First .. Last;`.
types-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints MIDDLE.
types-8.explain: The type is declared before the variable. After `begin`, `'Succ` moves `S` from `Start` to `Middle`, and then it is printed.
types-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
types-10.prompt: This program stops with `Constraint_Error`. Which line causes it?
types-10.explain: `90 + 20` is `110`, which is outside `0 .. 100`. Adding at most 10, for example `P := P + 10;`, stays in range.
types-11.prompt: This program stops with `Constraint_Error`. Which line causes it?
types-11.explain: `Positive` starts at 1, so it cannot hold `0`. Use `Count : Natural := 0;`.
types-12.explain: `Weekend'First` is `Sat`. A subtype keeps the positions of its type, and `Sat` has position 5 in `Day`.
records.title: Records
records.summary: Group related values into records, create them with aggregates, and keep records in arrays.
records.lesson.0: A **record** groups several values, which may have different types, under one name. Each part is a **component**. You declare a record type between `record` and `end record;`, and reach a component with a dot, as in `P.X`.
records.lesson.3: An aggregate sets all components at once. In a **named** aggregate like `(Name => "Ada", Age => 36)` you write each component name with `=>`. In a **positional** aggregate like `("Bob", 41)` the values follow the order of the components. A string component needs a fixed length, for example `String (1 .. 3)` for exactly 3 characters.
records.lesson.5: A component can have a default value in the type. `B := A;` copies all components, so later changes to `B` do not change `A`. `A = B` compares all components.
records.lesson.8: Arrays can hold records. `C (2).Price` reads the component `Price` of element 2. In `for It of C loop`, each `It` is a whole record.
records.lesson.10: Records work well as parameters. With `in out`, a procedure can change components of the record that the caller passes.
records.lesson.12: A component of type `String (1 .. 5)` holds exactly 5 characters. `"Pear"` has only 4, so it does not fit and Ada reports an error. Fill up with spaces, like `"Pear "`.
records.card.0: `type Point is record X, Y : Integer; end record;`
records.card.3: `C (2).Price` reads a component of an array element
records-1.prompt: How do you read the component `Age` of the record variable `P`?
records-1.explain: Components are reached with a dot. `'` asks for an attribute, and parentheses are for array indexes and calls.
records-3.explain: `B := A` copies the values. Changing `A.X` later does not change the copy in `B`.
records-4.statement: `=` compares two records component by component.
records-4.explain: Two records are equal when all their components are equal.
records-5.explain: A record type always ends with `end record;`.
records-6.explain: In a named aggregate, each component name is followed by `=>` and its value.
records-7.prompt: Build the declaration of a `Point` named `Start` with `X` 0 and `Y` 5.
records-7.explain: A declaration with a named aggregate: `Start : Point := (X => 0, Y => 5);`.
